packet.prompt:
Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

reader: Claude Opus 5.5, fresh subagent, prompt and images only; repository and search tools available but forbidden; exposures stated in each response
text:
PACKET-05 - unverified image-only first reading

Exposure statement: Nothing in my context revealed a proposed identification or reading of this fragment. The only labels seen are the modern pencil notes on the strip itself: "Stams, STA, Frg. 142r" / "142v", and a second pencil note on the recto that reads roughly "Aus Inkun[abel?] IV/48 vom J. 1636". I did not use that note to identify anything. Beyond the stated rules: I listed the packet directory to get the image filenames, and I made 2x enlarged crops of images 002-005 and 007-010 with PIL in my scratch directory to read small script. I opened no other files and used no web or search tools.

IMAGES
- image-001: overview, face 142r. A single long horizontal parchment strip, about 41 cm wide and 8 cm high (scale from the ruler). Ends are cut into pointed tabs. A fold or gutter runs vertically near the centre, where the pencil notes are.
- image-002, 003, 004, 005: native tiles across 142r, left to right. 002 and 003 overlap by about one column edge, as do 004 and 005; 003 and 004 overlap across the fold.
- image-006: overview, face 142v.
- image-007, 008, 009, 010: native tiles across 142v, left to right, with similar overlaps.

LAYOUT SURVEY (observations)
- The strip is a horizontal band cut across an opened bifolium (or two facing pages). Each face shows four text blocks: two columns left of the central fold and two columns right of it. That suggests a two-column layout per page. The outer tabs at both ends are blank margin. About 12-13 lines per column survive; tops and bottoms are cut through.
- Script: a small, compact book minuscule in brown ink with heavy abbreviation, including superscript letters, the 7-shaped et, the con- sign, and p-bar/p-cross forms. I make no claim about date.
- 142r: in the third column (image-004), a large red initial S spans about 4 lines. A red rubric in the right half of lines 2-3 reads "De Sobrieta[te] / (et) ... uigiliis" (see below). No other rubrication on this face.
- 142v: in the second column (image-008), a faded red initial (an F or P?) spans about 3 lines. A red rubric in lines 5-6 reads "In f[est]iuitate s(an)c(t)e? / Marie? v(ir)gi[nis]?" (uncertain).
- I see no running titles, interlinear glosses or marginal notes, apart from the modern pencil notes in the central gutter.
- Damage: a large brown water stain over the right half of col. 3 recto, which is the same area as col. 2 verso. There is a smaller stain at the left of col. 1 recto / right of col. 4 verso, plus a tear and small holes.
- At the lower left of image-002 a separately cut tab carries faint pale letters ("h[..]", "uera?", "hus q[..]"). These look like offset or show-through and not like main-text lines. They are not counted below.
- Tentative interpretation, from content only: continuous Latin prose in a homiletic/moral register (caritas, sins, vigils, sobriety). It is sectioned by rubricated headings. I make no identification.

CONVENTIONS
Line numbers count from the top of each image, including partly cut lines. (..) = expansion; ? = uncertain; [illegible] = unread; [ = word continues beyond the cut or column edge. Superscript abbreviations are expanded only where I am fairly confident; otherwise I give the letters.

AREAS READ AND UNREAD
- Recto col. 2 (image-003) and col. 4 (image-005) are the most reliable spans, with 12 connected lines each. The verso columns 3 and 4 (images 009 and 010) are the next most reliable.
- Weakest: recto col. 3, lines 5-12 (image-004, under the water stain), and verso col. 2, lines 7-12 (image-008, under the same stain). Most of their right halves are unread.
- Top and bottom lines of every column are cut through and only partly read.

LIMITATIONS
- I inferred the column order only from the physical position on the strip. I did not test which verso column backs which recto column, and I did not establish the original page order.
- Heavy abbreviation: many expansions above are proposals and are marked "?". The letters as written take precedence.
- A UV or multispectral image of the water-stained area (recto col. 3 / verso col. 2) would recover the most additional text. So would an image with stronger raking light of the top and bottom cut lines.
